blocks.x: LACAZE. You want a niche or two? LACAZE. LACAZE. Yeah, I'll tell you the name is a French name, but everybody try to pronounce it in English. LACAZE, LACAZE, and the right way is LACAZE. It spells LACAZE. Does it mean something in French? Do you know what it means? No, I don't know. It's one word. Yeah, one word. That way we always, everybody, you know, when doing any business with me, they always have that one word. It's not capital. Some people use a capital C. LACAZE, but it's

one word. That is easy. You don't spell it with a capital C. LACAZE. No, no. I see, because a lot of people have your name. No, I don't know. LACAZE. Yeah, well, I don't spell that one word. Let's get your name down, too, huh? Oh, my large, that is grown. Yeah, mine is Dick Allen. And, uh... Do you say the date? Yeah, what's the date, Mr. LACAZE, I can't remember? The date? Yeah.

What's it, it is? 26? I don't remember. No, it's the 27th. Let me, I got it on my watch. It's January 27, 1972. 27. Well, uh, you know, people used to get you mixed up with Bocard. Yeah, the name is Bocard. This is, that's why I just told you about the name, LACAZE and Bocard. A lot of Bocard, uh, they called me, thought I was Peter Bocard. Yeah. Because my name is Peter and his name was Peter. But he's a Bocard and I'm LACAZE. But he know you, because he told me about you. Oh yeah, yeah, I know him well, yeah. I know him well, worked with him quite a bit, you know, in the street bands. Oh yeah. Did you work with many street bands? Well, I never, not too many. But I guess I worked with everyone we had here at one time, you know. I might do one job or two jobs, but I never was a member. I remember one parade band that was Amos Riley. I don't know if you all have worked with him. Yeah, he's still a little bit on the west coast. No, no, that's Amos Riley.
Oh, that's Amos Riley. Amos Riley. Teddy Riley. Teddy Riley's dad.

I guess so. Yeah, look, Teddy was working in Cumberton Street. Yeah, his father, Amos. I worked in his band for quite a while, I mean, second and third trumpet. Did you ever work with the two-lane band? No, no, no, never worked with him. When were you born in Y.A.? Huh? When were you born? 1893. In Henry Orleans? Well, St. Bernard Parish, it's the next parish down here. What town? A plantation or town or a... No, St. Bernard Parish in town, that's the city part.
Yeah. But you were born, you weren't born on a plantation? No, no. What's your birthday exactly? What's your birthday?

July 14th, 1893. Quatorze, yeah. Yeah. You know what that is? A St. Bernard Parish. Yeah. Do you speak French? No, no. Did your parents speak French? Yeah, they did, but they didn't speak with us, with the children, because they used that, so they wanted to say something they didn't want us to know, they'd talk French, and that's why they were taught now. Did you know Jimbo from down there? No, I didn't know him personally, but I knew of him.
The clarinet play I'm talking about? Yeah. Jimmy Newman? Yeah, I knew of him, but I didn't know him. He was from down there, I can't remember, one of those big plantations, did he?
Yeah. He moved from one side to the other. I think he was from, I believe he came from around where they called Miroville. Mm-hmm. I think, I'm not sure, but I think it was somewhere around there.
Yeah, yeah. I know the Morgans were down there, and so many people were from Magnolia Plantation and Deerange and all those,
and then they all moved up to the city to play music. Yeah, well, I think the Durans, I think they were from down there too.
Oh, Maurice Durand? Maurice Durand, yeah. Oh, yeah. I see. I know, Jim Robinson told me he used to hear you were the Tuxedo and Excelsior brass bands.

Yeah, yeah. Yeah, that's right. You know Jim, call him Jim Crow? Yeah, Jim Crow, yeah. Yeah. Yeah, he used to be a bass player. No, no, no, no, the trombone player. Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. His nephew used to play bass. Little Jim. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Little Jim. Yeah.
Well, anyhow, back to your life and all I've kind of met, did your family play music in any way? No, no. I was the only one in the family that, uh,

took the music. And I started, I guess you'd like to know that, started trying to play a violin. And that was around in 1913. So I tried to play a violin when I kept it a couple of months with an instructor, somebody tried to show me. And I couldn't do anything with that. So then I changed my mind, and I got another instructor to show me how to play the trap drums. Mm-hmm. Because I liked that and thought I would do better. So I did do pretty good. I kept doing that for a couple of years. And something came up with this bus, trolley transportation. They didn't want you to ride on the street called the bass drum. Mm-hmm. So you'd have to hire a wagon to go everywhere you wanted to go and come back to it. And I couldn't afford that, because I didn't get enough money to do that. So then I had to leave that drums alone. And I had a friend in the band, who I was playing drums, was a trumpet player, which we just called his name, Maurice Duran. Oh yeah. He showed me the first finger, you know, of the trumpet. Then I got a teacher, tried to teach me how to play it. This man didn't play trumpet, but he played other instruments, see. And he showed me that. Do you remember his name? Yeah, his name was Professor Nicholson. Now the first name I don't know, Nicholson, that's all I can tell you. Was he in a certain school or something? No, he used to do this at his home. You know, he had quite a few scholars.
That must be Camille Nicholson's dad. Had a daughter named Camille? Probably so, probably.
He teach a lot of other musicians. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, I didn't know him, but I knew he had other scholars, quite a bit of other scholars there.
That's a famous family, that family. She's teaching there in Washington last year. Oh yeah.
She started the B-Shop music concert. So you started with the trumpet after 1913 then?

Oh yeah, after 1913. And I played with the food until 1934. Oh yeah. That's when you stopped? I stopped. I had a problem with my teeth. I had this pyrene disease. Oh yeah, gum. I was loose and I couldn't, didn't have no support for my lips. I had to leave the thing alone. Then I was kind of discouraged with it anyway, because that was making it harder to do by having these bad teeth. And he wasn't getting enough money. So I said, well, that's two things against me, not enough money and bad teeth. That's just where I leave it alone. You decided to stop playing music altogether? Altogether. You didn't play any other instruments? No, not since then. Never played enough. That's a long time ago. A long time ago. That's about almost forty years, ain't it? From 34 to now.
Yeah. Did you know Joe Oliver? He had problems.
Yeah, yeah, I know Joe Oliver. I know him, I might say well, I played in bands with him, parade bands, you know. Yeah. I know him.
Is this stuff for me to check to see if it's recording or something? Yeah. Okay.

I know Louis Armstrong somewhat the same way from playing in a parade band, you know. You see, most of these bands at that time, what I'm going to see, maybe somebody, others told him the same thing. But they was always shorter men. You know, they never had a full band. If they wanted fifteen men, twenty men, they had to start hiring some extras. So I was, if you could play any at all, it was a good thing. Or, it was somebody always needed you. See? So I got a chance to play with practically all of these parade bands that way.
You mean that there was such a need for players that you didn't have to be a very good recipient.

That's right, that's right, see? And I got a chance to play with practically all of these parade bands, you see? Sometimes one of the jobs, or two jobs, and maybe one never in the mood. See? And sometimes they'd say, you'll ask you to join the band, you see? Well, you'd accept that, you'd join the band. And maybe in a couple of months change your mind and join somebody else's band. And so that made you swap around. The band had a chance to work with these men.
You think that was more work than the musicians?

Well, yeah, they had more work than they had musicians for the work. See? We had plenty of work to do, but a little money. And I guess it was that we had with all kinds of business then. Plenty of work you had to do with money. But that gave me, what I said, it gave you a chance to play with these brothers. I played with Louis Armstrong in the Tuxedo Band, Parade Band. That was with Papa Celestein. I know you knew him. Oh yeah, I know him. It was his band. I played with Hank Heath and Louis Armstrong. See, I played the Tracking and Thurie. He and Louis, he was a leader. And Louis was playing solo. And then... That was the last band. Yeah. And then on another occasion, they had the Royal Garden. They used to have a dance up there every Sunday night. And on one occasion I had played the parade that day, and didn't have anything to do that night in the music line. So the man had the job in charge. I guess you know his name too. His name was Willie Johnson. Bunk, they used to call him. Bunk Johnson. So he asked me if I would rent Louis Mahon since I wasn't playing that night. Rent Louis Mahon so he could play a job for him. So I told him, well I'll do better than that. I let him use it. And I was a city of joy, you know. I was in love with music that much as sitting around there and enjoying the playing, see. So that's why I got real, you know, good acquainted with Louis on that night. And you knew Bunk, huh? Yeah. Yeah, I knew him. Set on a job with him for, when he was playing what they called Storyville at that time, playing on a job there. I was sitting on a job there, sitting on a job with him, listening to the band. Well I was very much interested in the band, and especially trumpet players. And anyone who could, any trumpet player who could play something, I would try and get what I could from him.
What trumpet players did you ever think were the best from him? Huh?
Which ones did you like the best of his trumpet? Well I'll tell you the truth, I have to say, Louis Armstrong was the one that I liked best out of all of them.
You mean from hearing him in person or from the records?

From, hearing him in person, both ways, you see. Yeah, I liked him better than all of them. And there was another one that was a sort of preference. I don't know if you heard of him. His name was Perez, Manuel Perez. Yeah, I liked his style in playing too. Very good. And I listened to his playing as much as much. I used to listen to him on Saturday night. My backyard and the backyard around the corner met like that. And they had, used to give a long party they called at the time. Never had no, and there was brass or something, and they'd stretch a tall podium and dance. Well I could listen to the band from my backyard. And this other man used to play there on Saturday night. Now they had a couple more musicians but I wouldn't remember who they was, you know, waiting with him on that job. Did you, where were you living then? At this time I was living in the 5300 on Dauphine Street.
Oh way down there.
5327 Dauphine Street. And this place was 816 Andrew what I'm talking about. The backyard gave to the backyard. You know I mean close enough to take the, the exodus that was going on.
Did you know Rene Baptiste and that bass player? Rene Baptiste, I know his name but I don't know him.

Big Dauphine player. Big Eye Louie, do you know him? Yeah I knew him well, real well. I knew him real well. Oh you knew him. Yeah, Big Eye Louie, he used to live, before he died he lived right around here on Dauphine by Calrott Street. But I knew him real well. I knew him from down in the Ninth Ward where I was raised.
He was down there in the Ninth Ward sometimes? Yeah. Yeah.
But who were some of the musicians in the Ninth Ward? Well, we had, let's see if I can remember, well Maurice Duran was from the Ninth Ward, and Joseph Watson was a clarinet player. stuff

He was from the Night Wars. And let's see who else. Charlie Bernard, he played a ghetto. He was from the Night Wars. And there's another man, I don't know, let's talk about the nickname. We called him Joe Hoodoo. He used to play trombone.
I heard of him.
From the Night Wars. You heard him? Yeah.
Yeah, I think he used to play with Willie Parker or somebody.
Yeah, yeah, that's right, yeah. Quite sure it was a, that Parker.
And Bruce was from down there too, wasn't he? Not as I knew of. No, I'm getting confused. He used to go down there, I think, with, with Mealy Barnes and Tom.
Yeah, he probably was, yeah, yeah.
And they used to go down into Delacroix Island and all those places.
Yeah, uh-huh.
Like, did you know Freddie Gould and Henry Ford and those?

Yeah, I knew them. Henry Ford, tell you the truth, if you're talking about the elder days, two Henry Fords, a young one and an older one. And the young one, he was a violinist. And I played drums with him for quite a while, you know, he had three or four, he didn't have a big orchestra, three or four people. And I played drums with him, Henry Ford, the young one. And the older one? And I knew the father, I knew the older one. What did he play? He was a bass violin player. Uh-huh, I see.

When you said you started playing drums in 1930, how long did you play drums for yourself? I didn't play too long, about two years, I think. And you started, you mean professionally, you were playing with bands? Yeah, yeah, yeah. And then you switched to the trumpet.
Switching the trumpet on account of what I told you, it was too much trouble to get around,
see. And what band did you start playing trumpet with, the first band?
The first band I played with, we organized a little band called the Supreme, the six people.
Who was in that band?
Well, let's see if I can, myself, and Edward Jackson.
What did you play?
He was a bass, he played bass violin and he played two balls.
What did he play with you? He played bass violin. Uh-huh.
And let's see who else was in that band.
Was that your band?

Oh, just Eddie and myself, we organized, you know, we got a couple of fellas together. You know some of these bands was organized and they last about, the organization would last about two months. But this band lasted longer than that. Oh yeah, that lasted for a couple of years, I think. And we had a woman playing piano with us, her name was, uh, uh, uh, oh, let's see, I can't go on there now.
Well, I could name some woman piano players. Well, name one that might be.
Camilla Todd, Mercedes, Homer Fields? Well, I worked with her too, I worked with her as a silver lead orchestra. Oh.
Mercedes, Homer Fields? No, she wasn't in that band. She wasn't in that band. No, she wasn't in that band.
She wasn't in that band. I see. It was May who used to play with Sam Morgan. No, not at all.
Wilhelmina?
Wilhelmina Bart, we called her. Wilhelmina Bart, Wilhelmina Bart, Wilhelmina the Ruiner, her name was, I think.

Yeah, she married the Ruiner and moved over across the river. Yeah, yeah. She was the one that played with her band. Yeah, that was the one that played with her band. Yeah, that was the Supreme Band. What about the clarinet's lady? Did you have a clarinet's name? Well, we have one, but I can't remember that name.
Did you ever work with a guy named Arthur on clarinet?
Yeah, Arthur Williams.
Oh yeah? Which band was that?
Well, I can't remember that. You know it's a little hard memory. Changes, changes aggregators, you know.
Do you remember the drum player, possibly?
No, I don't think I would.
He used six feet, you said. He had a drum.
Yeah, yeah, we had six feet.
And what happened with that band then, the last few years?

Well, you know, they separate one by one, somebody leave, and you know, you left, you who tried to keep the thing in mind, you left in the suit. And you had to start hustling some more. And you could always hustle a few, you know.
What band did you build after that?
Well, I went with a fellow by the name of Ernest Johnson, we used to call him, Doug Ernest.
Oh yeah?
Yeah. I don't know if you know about it. I guess you know about that. But he died up in Bowley. Yeah. Oh yeah. You know Dave Bailey?
Dave Bailey, yeah, he's a drummer.
Yeah, he told me about it. Yeah, he, he, Dave Bailey, last I saw him, he was doing janitorial work in Sierra Mill Hospital. Yeah.
Well, I don't talk to him too often. He's not too well, but his landlord, I know his landlord.
What about this first band, you said the Supreme Band, what year was that you think?
I don't think, I think it was around 1914, I don't know. Oh, it was that early?
Before the war anyway, huh? Yeah, yeah.
Well, during, I might say during the war, you know, around, between 1940, 70. I see, it was really early.
Yeah. Then you went with Dr. Robert.

Yeah, I worked pretty hard on the instrument. See, it might sound like I was making plenty of headway to you, but I was working like a dog to do it too. I was working day, I had a day job, and I was trying to do both, and I had to concentrate plenty on the trumpet, you know, in evenings from work, and all times I had on.
How often did the Supreme Band play? Did you play every night or?
Well no, I'll tell you, one time we played three nights a week. You know, dance hall, I think the name of the dance hall was, San Suci. Uh huh. Played three nights a week, yeah.
Where was that place?
That was on, uh, on Howard, I would say between Washington and 6th.

They used to have, I think, I've seen the letters in the sidewalk, or something, somebody pointed it out to me up there. I forget who it was, years ago. Yeah? Because I know where the place was, it's right there on Highway.
Yeah, on Highway between 6th and Washington. Yeah, I understand.
You know, uh, did you ever know a guy from down the river named Nene Cuoco?
No, Dene Cuoco. Ernest. Ernest. I know the name good. He was his trumpet player. You know, calling the name, it makes me like a older man, but I don't know him. He was Pills' brother.
Yeah, Pills' brother.

Pills, crippled Pills. We used to call, I never, I didn't know Pills' right name. What's up? Called him Pills, crippled Pills. You played with you? Yeah, I played with him for a long, you know, for the good while together.
What did they call him, Crowback or something? Crowback? Did you ever hear that nickname, Henry Rush?
Covett, Henry Rush, yeah. I might call him a personal friend, Henry Rush, he was a drummer.
Yeah, well he was telling us about it.
And then he played cornet one time too.
Did Russ play with your band? Russ, yeah, yeah. You mean the Supreme Band possibly?
No, Lola, we had a band called the Lola Band. That was with Eddie Jackson too. Eddie Jackson was a manager with my college, you know.
But anyway, you went to Duck Owners, and how long did you stay with anything?
Oh, I stayed with them for, I might say quite a few months, maybe six, eight months, maybe.
And then what happened?
Well, I can't remember where I went from Duck Owners. I don't remember.
But sometime after that you started the Lola Band then?
Yeah, yeah, sometime after that we started the Lola Band. That was the next band you had? I don't remember. I can't remember. Who was with Duck Owners in those days?
Who was the trumpet player before you? Before me, I don't remember.
Or after, huh? I can't even remember that. Yeah, yeah.

I know some people that played with him, you know, but it's hard for me to remember too, because Dave Bailey used to tell me all about that band. Yeah, yeah. And then Punch used to play with him at one time too, both of you. Punch Miller. Yeah.

Yeah, he played with him, he played with him quite a bit. And just, well that's different, he used to trombone player. Jack Carey, Punch Miller played with him quite a bit too. I played with Jack Carey myself quite a bit, but we never had an organized band, you know. But he would always, as much as possible, pick me to do the job whenever he had one.
Well, you know what about the time when you started in the old band, was that in the twenties? Or earlier? I've been, I was trying to remember that. Was it before the Depression, you think?
I can't, I can't see exactly.
Kind of hard, I tell you. Yeah, it's good.

Forty years, forty years ago, thirty years ago, it was kind of hard to remember. Especially the way this thing used to go, you know, you'd play with this band tonight, tomorrow night, playing some other band, you see.
But the Nola band lasted a pretty good long time.

Oh yeah, it lasted a long time. I think it lasted, I went out of business. All the way until you left? Yeah, quite sure. And I quit in 34, I quit the trumpet playing in 34, in 1934, and I'm quite sure it lasted

until I quit. You might have had a lot of different fellows in that band, they must have switched. Yeah, well yeah, you know, occasionally you change and you get somebody else. But Henry Russ talked to us about the Nola band. Yeah, he played a long time with the band. Do you remember anybody else that played in the band?
No, I can't remember nobody else right now.

You know, something I was thinking about a way to remember things is when the war is over with, you know, when they declared peace, when there's armistice, you might remember that. What were you doing then?

Well, I tell you, I never had to go to the war, so I don't, can't even remember that. I never went to the war, you know. They had some sort of a way to draft them by classes, I don't know, between class B or class A, some kind of way. And then it would be months before they called some of the people in that class, and kept you from remembering anything.
Oh yeah, I just thought maybe you'd remember that.
Yeah, I know, you would try to help me to remember, I know.
Did you ever play at the Capitol at Boat?

One time in my life, what time. I was called, just I'll tell you, shortage of people, I was called to take the place of a trumpet player. Well he wasn't in all the bands. No, no, no, I just called to do a job one night, one time. I see.
Who was on the boat then, what band?

Well, this fellow, the only one I can remember, a fellow called Faith Marble, who played the organophone. I think that's what you call that thing like a, played by Steve. The stereo. Yeah, yeah, he was playing. That was the only one I can remember. That was the only time I played on the Capitol. You said you had a day job with it. Yeah, well, you'll laugh at that. I was a blacksmith. Oh yeah? Doing wagon and carriage and cot days. I was a blacksmith. That was way back.
Oh yeah, that was way back. That was your first job?
Yeah, I was about seventeen years old and started to work at that.
How long did you stay on that?
Oh, I continued doing that until I retired now. I've been retired about fifteen years. Oh yeah?
Yeah.
Well, the business changed though, you know. They changed the automobiles and trucks and all. But it was similar, you know.
You still stayed in business? Eh?
You still stayed in business? Yeah, yeah. They kept it down.
Were there a lot of blacksmith shops in this neighborhood?

No, I never had too many. No. No. It wasn't too hard to get a job. If you knew how to work, that was what the people wanted. They didn't want that same thing about music. You want a good musician? You know, they want to hire somebody to try to get somebody who can do the work. That's the way it was in the back of the business. And I worked all the time. That's made it so hard for me, trying to play a music, trying to play a trumpet, and work too.
You never did like play every night then?

Yeah, I'll tell you one place now. I can't call, I could call the name of the man, ran the place. The name was Johnny C. Olena. He ran the place on Iberville between Wyvern and Royal. I used to have to go to work there at nine o'clock at night, work till four in the morning, and then try to work till the day.
That must have lasted too long. Well I'll tell you what happened, it lasted about six months. Oh yeah.

I'll tell you what made it a little better for me. I rented a room in town, see, close to where the day work was. And when I'd knock off from playing music at night, go to this room and I'd sleep the, excuse me, tell it was time to go to work today. It lasted about six months. Must have been really hard.
Oh it was tough.

Well what I used to do every night, tell you the truth, that's how I lost the job too. I'd get down off the bandstand about twelve o'clock, I'd go to the man's restroom, wash my face up and sit around there and take a nap. And the band manager, he got mad about that, and he got me fired. But I'm kind of glad he got me fired. I'll get some of that off there. I'll call his name, you might know him. His name is Eric Begaard. Oh yeah.
Oh that's right.
Yeah, yeah. He had a job in charge.
You were going into missions and taking a nap.

Yeah, yeah. See everybody at night. We were taking a nap. Well, they had a couple of entertainers around there, singers, dancers, and had a piano player. He was a man of piano. Yeah, I'll tell you. Hoyford Smith was a saxophone player, an alto saxophone, and Thomas Parker was playing the tenor saxophone.
Oh, they had two saxes.

Well, they had this on account of hard to find people, you know, musicians. I see. They had to keep what kind of kids. And there's one more I could remember. See, Parker, Hoyford Smith, I called them to you. They had a piano too, huh? And they had a piano. I can't remember his name. It was a man. I don't remember anything. And Ellie Begold, he was on the drum. Anyhow, there was about five. That's about all I remember. That makes fun, yeah. Yeah.
You said that was, did you, was that a reading band, or yes, a jazz band?

Well, it was kind of mixed up. Oh, they did have a few arrangements. Yeah. Yeah, yeah. I'll tell you what, I had to, wherever I went, I had to bring some arrangements with me, because I couldn't just do without it.
You know, I needed them, I had to have some music. I see. In other words, you played mostly for music.
Oh, yeah, see. I'd done some of this work without the music, but the biggest part of my work I'd done was with the music, you see.
In that place did you play for a show, or was it just dancing?

Well, it was, no, it was just a nightclub, like. And they had a couple of entertainers there to sing, some women, and do a little dancing. I don't know, I forgot the name of the club, but the man's name, his name was Cialina, Johnny Cialina. I mentioned that because I thought probably might.
We can figure out what that is. We can figure it out. From the location and everything.
Yeah.
Well, they've got books you can look, you'd be surprised at what you can look up in a book.
Yeah, I guess too.
Yeah, you know, working in the library, we have them. I knew you were a blacksmith.

Yeah, I guess too. They had that in a book? Yeah, I guess. You just... The city directory? Yeah, get it like, you get this information from me now. Yeah. And you talk to other people, and the people who know you, and they'll say, well I know that guy, he's a blacksmith. Yeah. Or he was a fisherman or something like that.
That was one of your longest jobs in music then. Yeah. Six months. Yeah, yeah, yeah, about the month of the long.
For a steady job like that, it must have been awful.
It was. It was pitiful.
Did you ever play at the place called the Music Box?
Oh wait, let's see, where was that located? Caronelet and Canal.
Yeah.

Yeah, I worked there a couple of weeks, it got too tough for me, because you had to continue, play continuously, you couldn't stop. You know, the, yeah, just like when I go to the sort of a Jitney style stuff. You paid for a dance and you couldn't stop, you'd take no rest. In other words, the way we'd done, we left the horns, play one chorus, and the balance of the instruments played the other chorus. Now people that were playing piano, they could play, you know, any time, all the time, because it wasn't so hard. But anybody who was playing the horns, clarinet, trumpets and stuff, you had to get a little rest. Yeah.
Yeah, I worked over there. What band was that with?
Well I didn't, there wasn't no band. I see. I was just, the Philly and the Blaze over there.
Yeah.
At the Crownlep Canal. Uh huh.
Was that the 20's you think?
Huh?
That's in the 20's? I don't know, I couldn't say.

It's hard to remember years. I couldn't remember. But uh, the man who, I think, had this job, was his original job, I think it was this fellow, Matwyer, Arnold Matwyer. Oh. I think he was the man with his, that was his job. When you took his place? I took his place for a couple of weeks. Oh I see.
Well he used to leave town. Yeah.
Uh huh.
He was on the play with Sir Hicks.

Yeah. Let me ask you a couple of names, see if you remember his father. Do you remember Charles McCurdy? Charles McCurdy, yeah. He used to be with Roeby Show's orchestra. Uh huh. He played with you too?
Well, uh, Kev, didn't he?
Yeah.
He wasn't, he wasn't a steady member.
No. What about Riccardo-Lexis?

Well, Riccardo-Lexis, him and I was pretty good friends, and we played together in places, you know, uh, on Exceptional's, you know, if we had an exception we might play together. And then we played the street together too. I see. Yeah. What about Harrison Barnes?
Yeah, uh huh. He was a block in one of the old bands, Enola.
Uh huh. He was a trombone player there. Yeah. I know him real good too. In the Enola band. Yeah. Uh huh. What about Red Allen? Allen? Not the old man Allen. Well, no,
We used to call him Red Allen, the young fella.

because it makes plenty of people lazy. Did you like to work when you were 14? Yeah, I like to work. I used to go to work with a good heart. And what kind of work were you doing?

Well, I was helping me in a blacksmith shop. First, I was in a drug school, getting 50 cents a day, 50 cents a week to go deliver orders of the druggish. What did your parents do, your father and your money? Well, my father drove a team of horses. Well, they delivered a delivery wagon. I'll tell you what, like this Wilson and Company or Homo people. Well, he worked for a company of that sort, but sold wholesale meats. I mean, deliver. We can stop it. He's consigned. I used to deliver this meat at night. What was his name? His name was Peter Lacazzo. I heard of Meat Man's feet. That's a wreck. No, that's something different.
Yeah, that's something different. That's something different. So, in other words, you didn't go into your father's business?

No. No, I went, tell you what happened. I went to that place where he worked one day, and I tried to walk around in there, and it was very slippery there. No. No, just because I loved it. I see myself go on jobs where somebody else is working and take over for them just to be doing it. Oh, yeah.

I'll ask him, the guy lives near me. Yeah. The guy lives near me, I don't have to get up.
You don't have to get up. Let's see if I, huh? You don't have to get up.

Let's see if I can't walk. I'm kind of sick, you know.

No, no, that was after him. Oh, after him. So that must have been, uh. You see, it was a different Silverleaf. It was a different man handling this thing. Well, who was handling it then? I don't know, no. But Albert Baptiste had it when I was, uh, playing with him. Yeah.
Well, I think he had it when Hippolyte Charles. He probably had it.

I know he had it.

Yeah.

I think she was. I'm not sure. Was she with the band when you came in? With the Silverleaf Band? No. She wasn't with the band. I think she was with them then. When she was with him? It does. With Albert Baptiste, Silverleaf Band. Yeah. I think she was with them when Hippolyte Charles was playing.
I guess she had gone on with Radzli by then. Probably so. She started with Radzli for years. Yeah.
Yeah. Ah, that's right. Talking about Silverleaf, what was the Silvertone Band then? I don't know. Was that one of your bands?
I don't know, no.
Well, when did Henry Russ mention that? He said he played in the Silvertone Band. He must have maybe, maybe he's mixed up on that.
He probably got mixed up on that. He played with Silverleaf. He played with the Silverleaf Band. Yeah, he played with us.

Sam Dutry Sr., he played with me quite a bit. You know, we was practically in the same age group. And we were pretty good friends. And he played with me quite a bit. He never was a member of the band. He played with us quite a bit.
I think Harrison Bonds told me about him.
Huh?
I think Harrison Bonds told me about the old man dude. Yeah. The one I knew was quite young.
Yeah, yeah, the one you knew was quite young. And he died. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
The young Sam just died on the job.
Yeah, that's right. Yeah, but the other one's been dead quite a while. Oh yeah, yeah.
And Lord's been dead a while.
Lord's been dead a while too, yeah.

Arthur Williams? No, I'll tell you the truth. I can't remember if he played with anybody regularly, but I know he played with me in different bands, you know. We played together in different bands. What instrument did he play with? He was a clarinet player, Arthur Williams. No, not as I knew of. And Camilla Todd?
Camilla Todd used piano players.
Did you know her? Yeah, I knew her well. I mean, you know, we worked together quite a little while.
What was it like to work on that capital boat?

Well, yeah, I worked pretty hard. Well, that band was strictly a reading band.
Yeah, well yeah, yeah. They did. They did none at all by that. That is they all had it in front of them. I didn't get them to look.

No, they used stock arrangements. Yeah, they used them.
How many bands did you play with that had special numbers arranged from?
Well, I don't know, I'll say about three or four. That's all right.
They have their own arranges in the band?
Yeah, yeah.

No, on a copy. I was writing on a copy.
Oh, when you were at the Pelican, how many bands would they have there?

At Pelican, sometimes they would have two. At times they'd have what they call a jazz festival, I think they called it that. They'd have two bands, you know. One playing opposite the other. Have like a battle? Well, they'd have like a battle, yeah. You know, one band do some playing and the other one rests up and leaves another one, the other one breaks it, do some playing. Wasn't there Tik Tok around there too?
Huh? Didn't they have a place called the Tik Tok? I don't know.

That may have been later. I wouldn't say that might have been later. Well, what were some of the bands that were there? Did Bebe Ridley ever work at the Pelican? Anybody know? Bebe Ridley worked there sometime, yeah.
He worked there with the tuxedo band.

think his brother's going to bring him in. Yeah. Wow. Who else? I don't know. Out of town bands? Oh yeah, they had one time an out of town band. If I could call the name of that you would know that. It was from somewhere up in the country, you know, not too far from
here. Oh, I forget the name. Well, let's see, they had the Clabin Williams

Clabin Williams. Clabin Williams was the one I want to talk about. They was there sometimes. What about Bud Scott? Well, when Bud Scott was there I wouldn't know about him. But you knew him. You knew him? Yeah, I knew him. From Natchez, I'm talking about that. Would he ever come to
know him? I don't know. He's from Baton Rouge. Yeah, I don't know him. Yeah, well Bob Thomas and Captain
