Club, was that up then? Yeah, that was up at doing good. I mean, you know, they were having some of the things that were there, but they were, in some instances they're regular. I played quite a bit there. Where was the Autocrat then? Oh, right where it is now. Right where it is? Right where it is, that's the same spot. Oh, yeah. It was different buildings. Well, they had been adding on to the building, you know, they remodeled the building and all, but it's the same building. It's the same building. It's the brick building, no? Yeah, they, and they adding on some steel structure I see over there, adding on one on this side. Was it, it wasn't the brick building, no, way back then? No, it was a wooden building, way back then, I wish I could. And they had, what bands did they have? They had your own, huh? Yeah, we had a band there. They had other bands, but I couldn't call their name now, you know. Did you ever work at the Bulls Club? Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. They had a rampart in six. Yeah, I worked there several times. Quite a bit. Yeah.
Most, most, most of your jobs was in these different clubs like that. Yeah. The San Su? Mm-hmm. San Su-Sea, San Su-Sea.

Yeah, that was over there on, on Howard Street, yeah. Did you always play for dancing, you know? Yeah, pretty much, yeah, for dancing. Yeah. Did you ever hear of the Lions Club? The Lions Club? I heard of it, but where it was, right now, I couldn't see.

You never saw that club? No. What about the Hop Goblins? I heard about them, too. But you never saw that? No. Well, what, down in the Ninth Ward, what did people do? Did they have trades down there? In the Ninth Ward? Yeah, what was it down there?

Well, they had dance halls down there, around Independent, around Independent Street. Then they had, uh, this place that I'll tell you about, this, uh, what they call it now? Oh, they have dancing in the breeze with the tarpoli, or the lawn dance, or something like that. They did that down there. Did they have trees, and dance under the trees? No, they were just, just, it was just an empty lot, and they covered it with the tarpoli and the dance. Did you ever play outdoor jokes with your band? I'm not talking about grassland. No, not, oh, yeah. I used to be talking about something, it reminded me. All the outdoor stuff I ever done was in, at Lake Punch and Train. Oh, I see. In these camps, they used to have camps out at Millenvoig, they had camps in West End, and they had camps in this other place out there, Bandit Fort. And during the summer months, it would be a rare thing to be on a Sunday. You'd go to work by ten o'clock in the morning and wait till six in the evening, in one of these clubs. You'd be in one place or the other, either Banish Fort, West End, or what you call it? That's the only outdoor work I ever done. And that wasn't exactly outdoors, because all these places have, uh, I might call it a shade. They all had a... Like a pavilion? Yeah, yeah. The oak,

Yeah, practically all of them had that. How was out at Spanish Fort Sunday looking at it? Yeah. How does it look? Well, there's nothing there except the ruins, you know. Yeah, yeah. But, but they must have had something out there more than that then. Yeah. And you know, people have built up new homes. Oh, you know, yeah. Yeah, but what was there?

Well, they had, well I'll tell you, the people had camps, what they call them. They had small houses, small buildings, what they used for Sundays and some of them used for vacation. That's on the edge of the bayou? On the lake itself? On the edge of the bayou and on the lake too. Oh, I see. Yeah. I guess what you said, you see the ruins out there, you must see some of these platforms that they had, built from the wharf to go out. Most of the camps was on the water. Oh, I see. And they had a platform from the, from the wharf to walk out to the camp.
At Spanish Fort all night, it looks like bricks from the actual fort itself. Yeah. Oh, yeah. That's Spanish Fort itself. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Fort St. John. Yeah. When you played, you say you played all day from 10 to 6? Yeah, from 10 to 6, 10 in the morning to 16.

You think it was a hard job? Well, no, I'll tell you how that was. Wait, now that was a little decent. Because, you see, during the day, the people would stop to eat, some stopped to go swimming, and so on, so the band wouldn't have to do nothing. You know, while the people would stop to eat. Did they feed the band? Oh, yeah, yeah. They gave you all the drinks, food, about, excuse me, about six dollars a day, and all the food and drinks you could eat. Was that good pay? Well, I'll tell you. Well, I'll tell you. That was the best you could do. And everybody was paying about the same, so.
It was a pretty good job, you thought. Yeah, yeah, it was a pretty good job.

I mean, because it was always a very long job, you know. Yeah, yeah, from 10 to 6, you put it on, just eight hours. But I have to tell you, you'd get a time to rest, you know, while people went to swim, or stopped to eat.
You, the people would be dancing to your music at that, or you just entertained?

Well, they did dance, and people would be dancing under this pavilion, under this porch they had, like, all around the building, and dance on that floor all around the building. Were those private parties, or were they hired? Well, they were, they was, uh, practically all private parties, uh, uh, people wanting to do something, to have some fun on a Sunday, and they'd get together and do that. Would it be like, some kind of club? No admission, no admission, some, some clubs, yeah. But they weren't charging no admission. I mean, how many people would there be there, like? Oh, sometimes they had pretty good business. I wouldn't, couldn't estimate right now, but, well, pretty good business.
Did you ever play at Lucian's Pavilion? Lucian's Pavilion, I've...
It's on the lake, on Millenheim. Oh, that's around, uh, Frenchman, around the lake on Frenchman Street.
It's supposed to be on... Well, I mean, at that time...

Around Millenberg, something like that. Around Millenberg, yeah, around Frenchman, like I said, religion field of Frenchman, around there. Yeah, right in there. Yeah, I played it there one time, I mean. They used to, people used to use it practically every Monday, for some sort of a banquet or something. Yeah. And Querellis, did you ever play that? No. No.
I think it's Shockey's Cousins. They probably mainly used Shockey. I don't know. And what about the trades? What kind of trades did people have down in the Ninth Ward?

Like, the different musicians, did they work days? Well, some of them worked in carpentry business, you know, and some... done some kind of work where they wasn't compelled to go to work every day. Mm-hmm. So, in case they had to stay out at night too late, they'd just be able to stay home.
They'd done that time. Do you think that most musicians that you associated with and play with,

did they, most of them have other jobs? No, they didn't. I was... I used to be the only one. Sometimes we'd be five or six together, and I'd be the only one who had to work. Next day, yeah. Balancers, and... was... all from work, you know. Most of them had just... they only played music. They played music, and I wondered how they done. Sometimes they played for a dollar and a half tonight, and they didn't work the next day. I don't know how the hell they done.
They must have worked more than you did, and they tried to work every night if they could.

Well, they did. Plenty of them worked, tried to get an every night job if it was possible. Was it possible? But you couldn't give. Well, sometimes, but not often. Couldn't get an every night job. They... in that way they made a lot less money than you did. Well, they did. Yeah. That's what I say. I wondered sometimes how they done. Because I could hardly make it all... I was working each day doing that at night, and I could hardly make it all. I don't know how they done. But some people just don't give a damn.
Well, in the wild works, some of them have rich wilds.
I don't know. Maybe so.
But what about trappers? Was anybody a trapper that you knew down there?

Well, I didn't know. They had some down there, but I didn't know them. I just know about people saying what they do, you know, for a living. They trapping, picking moss and do trapping. The moss, they had a club. The moss pickles and the coon trappers. That was the name of the club, and they all used to congregate there. Did you play for them? No, I never did play for them. What kind of people were they? Well, they were all right. They were... Page okay? Oh, yeah, okay. They were... Just ordinary people. And you didn't have to be afraid. No. Well, you know, now sometimes if you...

I was talking... Do you know Kid Shee, Koloff? He plays trumpet with the Olympiad man. He was saying that he was playing down in the Ninth Ward, and that second line said you're going to have to share that money.
Oh, no. You know? You know, the people do so many different things. Now, they didn't do then. But I never heard of them doing anything like that. But I wouldn't say that they wouldn't.
In your day, you said there weren't very seldom problems when you played in a place, like a fight.

No, no, no. Very seldom. And all you do, they have a system. They let the band play a little tune while they're fighting, and then somebody would go over there and quit the fight, you know. Stop them. Well, I never had any serious problems. No, no. Not shooting nobody. One place I went up in St. John's Parish, and they had a group of people in there. First time that ever happened to me, a group of people was there, and they had some sort of a sisal there pinning a flower or something on you to identify, you know, see if you peel your hair, come in. And so they caught a couple of them sneaking in like that, and they made a fight, and they started to shoot, you know. They shot about five times in the place. And I tell you the truth, they had about 400 people in that place. And I don't know where they all went when the shooting started. But after the shooting was over, they see the little rooms that's coming out. I don't know how they ever gotten there. But that was the only time anything serious ever happened to me when I was playing music. But I didn't move or I stood on a New York stand and said, wherever I go I might get shot. So I stayed right there. You never had any... And the bass player was Eddie Jackson. He stooped behind the... Behind the bass, you know. A straight bass about thick as people. Yeah. And he was behind there. It wouldn't do him any good.
It's better to get underneath the piano, but I guess you didn't have any piano to get on the bass. No, they didn't have none there.
So you never had any problem like going home from a job where you get robbed or something like that?

No, no, never. And I went home from any direction in town. And plenty of times I had to walk because all the traffic, all the, what you call it, all the transportation, was quick. About one o'clock at night. And you had, no matter where you was, where you lived, if you wanted to get home, you had to walk. So I walked and went through any kind of neighborhood, you know, nobody was.

You never heard of any musicians really having trouble like that? No, I never heard of anybody, no, no. Or badly treated or beating them up with anything. Nobody, no. That happened to Rick and Alexis, didn't it? Rick and Alexis got beaten up in his mouth, so he had to stop playing trumpet.

Oh yeah, uh, that happened to him. I don't know how that, some people he was playing and praise, and they, they tell me they met him on the street. Yeah, and beat him up with a tired tool or something. And couldn't play trumpet no more after. But he can't, after you, if your teeth are gone, or your jaw are gone, you can't play that damn thing when you got on anything.
You never heard of anybody else happen like that? No. That was the only one I ever heard about happening with him. I never heard of anybody else.

Did you belong to the Musicians' Union? No, I never did. There wasn't a strong group? Well, they was, try to organize a union then. And, uh, they wasn't doing anything with it, you know, just skipping about with it. What bands were in the union? Were there any bands in there? Well, they had a few bands. I remember a couple of fellas talking about it. They had some kind of meetings, but they never did, uh, they never did come to anything with it. Until we later then, this musician later, you know, talking about it.
Yeah, because now the union is pretty strong.
Yeah, yeah.
Did you travel much? No. You never did get, did you play up in, uh, Jefferson Parish, or?
Yeah, I played Jefferson Parish. St. Charles. I went around in the... stuff

Oh, you did go out state? Yeah, Mississippi a couple of times. Texas? Yeah. I didn't, I never went to Texas, no. Hardly ever went out of state, though. How did you get a job out of town? Well, now, somebody from in town would know somebody in the place, and they inquire about a band, and you get in contact with them, then they get the arrangement needed for you. Oh, I see. Yeah. That's the way it was done.
But you couldn't go really because you were working a day job.
Working a day, there was always somebody who wouldn't go, but some of these people who
wasn't working, they needed the job so bad they'd go anywhere. And they'd get somebody in the place.
Yeah, that's right. They'd go by my place. And I didn't mind.
Did you ever play in any markets or stores or anything?

Not, no, no. I heard of that. Reggie they used to tell me. No, I never did. You used to play advertisement for them? Oh, yeah. You see, I played, I have time, way back, a few days, using wagons and horse to go around. That's the time I was playing drums, though. But that was a weird, you know, beginning. I never played no trumpet on, no, no, half a time. Not as I can remember.
Well, what was the market like in those days? I mean, I think.
Well, it was, it was, the market we had here was like, I'll say a building with four posts and a roof.
No oil. No oil, that's right. And what did they sell then?

Well, they had these stands built up, but all that was open. They stayed open day and night. See, and I didn't have trouble nobody didn't steal them. That's the only way they did it. They still wanted to start it closing or later, start it closing, you know, you see.
How much longer do we have left of it?
It was only a minute or so. I want to ask you, you never did get to play with the WPA band then? WPA band then. You quit.
And that's the time you quit. That's the time you quit. Yeah, that was, by the round, about the same time I quit playing music.
And you knew Lewis Jermaine pretty well?
Yeah, I knew it pretty well.
And you couldn't get in the band?
Couldn't get in the band, no. I guess a lot of people were trying to get in the band.
Yeah, I think that was the trouble. I think they had some, some, some, they didn't need none. Yeah, but you must have been a better trumpet player than some of the guys in there,
because some of them were just ham.
Well, I know, I know that, but let's go back to this politics, political. I think the thing was being done like that, too, you know. You had to know somebody. Yeah. And if you didn't know nobody...

Do you think, talking about that, do you think that, you know, most persons were like that, a band, when they hired people, did you necessarily hire them because they were good musicians, or because they were his friends? Well, no, no.

Most of them, they hired them because they could play music, but they needed them. They needed musicians. You see, it was a kind of hard matter. This is what you all was talking about before. Most of these musicians was, couldn't qualify as musicians, because they couldn't read. So that made the ones who could read, that give them a chance to be hired, if possible. But when they got enough of these others, when they figured they had enough to read and they could get along with it, well they wasn't particular about whether you could read it or not, see. And then you had this. People, some of the people who were at the head of the thing, they didn't read, they didn't care if nobody else read.
You think most bands didn't read? Huh? Most bands that you know did not read.

Didn't read. No, that's right. And you know, it was comical about that. You'd go to someplace, for instance, when you came here, and you brought your band, and you'd set up your band to get ready to play. And you'd set up a music rack, you know, to put the sheet on. The people all start looking at you, see? They don't know what they're doing. They're going to play their old note music. Hey, we don't want that. They say it out loud. Oh, people didn't want that.
No, they say it out loud. They say it out loud. You see, the crowd did not like the band. No, they didn't.
No.
They wanted a band that's a place.
Yeah. Yeah. They're going to play their old note music, we don't want that.

And you had to put up with that, it was there, you know, how high it is. But could you do them? You couldn't do them. That leads me to another question. The places that you played with, was they mostly Negro places, or mostly white places?
Well, no, I'll tell you, I was lucky. I was lucky. I played mostly white places. Better paint.
Better pay.
Better pay and better treatment. I had to hate to say that about my own people. I've got to tell the truth. Since you all are here for this interview, I've got to tell the truth. My people was awful.
Well, they didn't have much money in the first place.
Well, that was one of the bad things. They didn't have money to do things what they would want to do. And then some of them just didn't want to do nothing right.
They didn't want to do it right. You mean when you played in Negro places, there was a rougher... Yeah, that's right.
...less money, no bonds, etc. Yeah, that's right. Yeah. They wouldn't even give you sand if they could help them. Well, that has to do with...
With no boat races.
With no boat races, yeah.
Well, it's a money situation, it's because they didn't have money.
Did you play in Irish Channel?

Yeah, I played Irish Channel every time. See, when I was playing music with Ernest Johnson, Doug Ernest, he lived down in Irish Channel, around St. Thomas Street. And he used to get white... He knew these people out there, see. And he used to get white from these people, whatever dances they had. They were pretty quiet bunch of people?
Yeah, they were nice people. I didn't find nothing wrong with them. No?
No.
Did they give you a nice... Oh yeah, yeah, yeah.

The only thing we had to do was what I'm saying every now and then, a couple of these youngsters would start a little fight, and they'd say, play music, bands play music, they're fighting. All I had to do was play any little thing, you know. Couple of boys or anything, and then stop the fight. No fight, no trouble, we never had no trouble.
Did you ever play for any Germans?
Well, I'll tell you the truth, I wouldn't know. You wouldn't know, huh?
No, I wouldn't. But I guess they had plenty of Irish up there.

Yeah, they had plenty of them. Well, I would say yes, if I didn't see one, because I know that was the place they supposed to be living. Yeah. Irish people were supposed to be living out there, so I would think they had plenty of them. Did you ever play at the Santa Center Club? Santa Center Club? Once or twice. Not often. Did you ever know any Creoles? Oh, I got some of you in my family, but I...
Do you call yourself a Creole?

Yeah, but I don't, I can't talk that language anymore. No, but I mean there's a lot of people that don't talk that language. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Like Lonnie Furgo. Young ones, yeah. He don't speak. No, the young people who avoided talking in that Creole stuff. The grandparents and all were talking. Yeah, but... All of my parents were talking, but none of us.
But they didn't, you didn't ever hear any Creole singers?
No, no.
Like Didi Pierce? Yeah, yeah. Did he? Yeah, yeah, I know him, yeah. He sings great. And Albert Burbank?
He was a trumpet player, Didi. And Albert Burbank? I can't think about the name of the song he mostly sang. Albert Burbank too. Yeah, he la va. Did you ever sing any of the songs?
No, I never even tried.

Did you sing anything? I used to sing choruses practically every song. Oh, yeah. The chorus, but since then I got, I had an accident. I inhaled some, I'm doing some soldering, and I inhaled some fumes from the soldering, and it damaged my lung to a certain extent. I go to the hospital now, but it damaged my lung to a certain extent, and I can't sing. You never did go for treatment? Yeah, I go to the hospital now. You still have to go? Oh, yeah. How long ago that happened? Oh, that happened about, maybe fifteen years ago. And it still bothers you? Yeah, occasionally I have trouble. Oh, with your breathing? I have a bad, have trouble breathing.
Oh. What happened when you get, when the accident happened? Did you get very sick right after? Well, no, I never get real sick, but... You didn't go to treatment right away?
No, no, no.
No, it didn't go to treatment right away.
Oh, that's probably the problem.
That's probably the problem.
Otherwise, I had pretty good voices singing. I'd sing all the choruses.
And people liked that, they wanted you to sing? Yeah, they liked it.

How did you sing without microphones in those days? Well, I'll tell you what, we used to have a... A megaphone? Yeah, yeah. A big piece of paper pulled up like a funnel, and you sing through there. I mean, that was the only way you could spread the voice out. Like today, you've got a microphone, now you can use that. Right.
I'm talking about Creole singers, do you remember any other musicians that used to sing in Creole? Who was that? They used to sing in Creole. Do you remember any?
Oh, no, no, I don't remember when I was singing that.
Who else was Creole of the early 25th?
Well, let's see. I guess Maurice Durand, Perez? They were Creoles, huh? Quacko?
Yeah, yeah. They were Creoles.
Did you play mostly with Creole musicians, you think, or...?
Oh, I played with any kind. Anything? Yeah.
You say Louis Caput knows you, huh?

Yeah. You work with him, then? Yeah, I play with him on occasion, you see. In other words, now he's an older musician than I am, but he wasn't too old for me to play with. You know, what I mean is this, for instance, you lots younger than I am, but if you was a trumpet player and I'm a trumpet player and I need one, I get you, I mean afterwards you could say, well I play with people. Yeah, yeah. You know?
He used to work with Earl. Earl used to play with him.
Yeah, I played with Earl, huh? Yeah. That's before you done it.
Yeah.
Well, it's the next one.
Well, since you run out, do you ever play with the Magnolia Band? No, never did.

I knew of the Magnolia Band. I know Louis Caput was with him, I thought maybe that was the same. You didn't know Caput's brother. Freddie? Yeah. I knew him like this, to the public. You never met him. No. Somebody say that's Freddie Caput. And then I'd see him on different occasions and I'd recognize him, see. But for me to know him, I don't know him, but I knew Louis. Did you hear him play? Did you hear him play? Oh yeah, Freddie, yeah. Oh you did? Oh yeah, I know, I heard him play lots of times. And I thought he was a nice trumpet player.
What band did he play with? Oh, let's see if I could call the name of the band, Olympica, believe me.
Yeah, Olympia. Yeah. Yeah.
You thought he was very good?
I thought he was very good.
Was he very popular here?

Yeah. Oh yeah. You see, that was one of the things, you know, people did this. If a group of people recognize you as being able to do something, other people follow the group. You know, like if I come along and say, well, Albert is a good trumpet player, and somebody heard me say that, they'll say the same thing. The first thing he gets a big bill up, you see, and that's the way these people used to
do it. Which trumpet players were the most popular one?
Well, when Louis Armstrong was here, he was the most popular one. You see, he left here after a while. Sure, yeah. Freddie left here too.
Yeah.
When he was left, he was left. What about Joe Oliver?
Joe Oliver was good too.
He was really popular. Yeah, yeah, he was good. Well, what about somebody like Rene? Would he be more popular? Rene, he was real good too.
He was popular too with the people. But would he be more popular in the seventh war than he would in the third?
Or how did that happen? Well, no. He had his response. No, that wouldn't make no difference. Yeah, he wouldn't have his special bunch.
That's right, yeah. But do you think that some, like, some of the things were popular in certain places? Certain sections, yeah.
Yeah, like if someone was popular in the white.
Yeah, and some of the black.
Yeah, but it wasn't like that with him. He was the same anywhere.
Who was? Anywhere he put her in the air.
I mean, you know, he would.
He did well. Excuse me. He didn't. He didn't. Well. Well. Well. Well. Well.
Well. Well.
Well. Well.
Well. Well. Well. Well. Well. Well.
Well.
Well.
Well. Well. Do you think that some of the musicians that played strictly in colored places? Huh? Some musicians that only played in colored places? Or? No.

I don't think there was anyone only played in colored places. No. No. I don't think that. You see, there was a funny thing here in the South. I mean, we have a lot of colored people who say, well, they don't like me cause I'm black. And they wouldn't have me over there if I was black. But that's not so. among the people. They don't care what color you are. If you can do something alright, they recognize you as a person. And that's the way it was with that. So, the fellow was a good musician he would be like. Yeah, like, yeah, no matter what his color was.
What about boxers and sports and things like that? Would they recognize you?
Well, yeah, yeah, they recognize you. But don't you think that like in the black places they would like a certain type of music than you would like? Well, I'll tell you, I just
told you about that. That would happen no matter. If you was playing a type of music that they didn't like, they didn't give a damn just black or white. Right. Like if you played in the black.
wouldn't you play a little different type of music? Well what you do, you feel the people out,

we call it. You play something and try them, see. Play some kind of tune, see if they liked it, well you try again. If they liked it, it went on. But if you could tell first two or three tunes whether they liked it or not, and then you'd go change or something you'd think they would like. And then after you find out what they liked, well then you would just do the same thing for the time
you'd think. Because like if you play in a more high class play you would play more sophisticated music. Well sophisticated music, but the thing had got

so with that, those people wanted the common music. You had to put them in the alley too? Yeah man, they wanted that. They wanted the blues? Sure, they'd come tell you too. Yeah, they didn't want it to be too polite. Too polite, yeah, they didn't want that. People got like that about that.
Did you belong to, do you belong to many societies and clubs now? No, I don't belong to one. I see your picture in the weekly sometimes, you know. Yeah, but I don't...
It's been a good while. I don't, they might have got, somebody might have had something to say about.
Yeah, yeah, maybe it was a carnival portal or something. Yeah, it must have been, because I don't belong to them.

You don't belong to them, you're not a big joiner? No, no, I don't belong to nothing like that. Did you ever belong to make insurances or...? Well I was, at one time, I used to be a salesman for Unity Insurance Company. Oh, I see. And then I was known widely from that, with the other companies too, you see. You know, the companies, they, they pretty much all, the agents pretty much know all, all agents from other companies. You meet them on the street, see. Yeah. Yeah. I knew plenty of people like that too.
Tony Fugero is one, you know him? Who? Tony Fugero. He's right, but he used to play in mixed bands here and there. Yeah, I don't know him at all lately. You know him if you saw him.
Were there, by the police, me to ask you, were there any mixed bands in the way back when you started?

No, they used to have them like this, but they didn't know it. In other words, if a fellow was colored and he was bright enough to pass, he would play in any band. Because what they wanted, I just told you, they wanted somebody who could do the job. And no matter if he was colored as long as he was bright enough, you know, so it don't make the confusion, well they'll take him. Do you remember? Yeah, I remember one, Arnold Matoia was one. And Dr. Eddie Cherie, Eddie Cherie was one. He was bright and he played in the band. He played in the white band. And Matoia. And Matoia was one. They might have a few others, but I wouldn't know, you see.
They had plenty of others. Yeah, but I didn't know. Yeah, I know, but you know, you'd be surprised. See, all the white musicians knew that.

Yeah, but they knew it. But they wouldn't have admitted. They wouldn't have admitted to public. As long as the fellow was bright enough to pass, they didn't care. See? But like you said, they wouldn't admit it. They would have admitted there, somebody said, well you playing that band with that nigger. You say, well I don't know he's a nigger. I mean, but he did know. But he said he did. He was covering up for his friends. That's right. That way they had plenty of them. What you say they had plenty of them done. But I knew these two.

Yeah. Did you know Johnny Lawler used to be a butcher in the market? Yeah, I knew of him. I didn't know anybody knew of him. Yeah, he used to be a trumpet player. And he'd tell me about how Arnold Macario would make a mistake, Macario. Yeah. He'd play a funeral in the afternoon and then could play a white job at night. At night, yeah. And get in trouble because he was a white job.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Because, yeah. I knew that, for the reason they called me their name, because I knew this was too personal.
Oh, yeah. Would everyone have any white assistant played in black bands?

Well, I wouldn't know. You see, this is what I say, because the white man does this. He can't pass the white. No, he can pass quicker than me. Oh, yeah. Because they got plenty of Negroes who look like white people.
Oh, yeah.
See, they got plenty of Negroes resembled white people, so all they have to do is say, well, he's colored, he just look like that. You know, his associates.

Oh, he could play with the light-skinned band. That's right, sure. But you wouldn't even know then. No, you wouldn't know. You don't remember any of them. No, I don't know. No, I don't know. No, I don't know now. You didn't know Sidney Ayrton, huh?
No. He used to play with Lee Collins in the quarter. Yeah. I knew Lee Collins. In the 20s.
You know Achille Bakke? Achille Bakke? I knew of him.
Well, he used to pass for our two things.

Yeah, well now there was a George Bakke too. Yeah. That was his brother. But he couldn't pass, I don't believe he was white enough. No, but Achille must have been lighter than him. Yeah, he must have been. Yeah. George Bakke, I knew him good too.
I never did play with him, but I knew him good.
That's what you knew a lot of musicians that you never played with.
Yeah. You used to go around and listen. Go around them, you see. I love music and I wanted to learn. I go to these places and I get acquainted with the fellas, you see.
Let's go to the alley and get a drink.
Yeah, did you ever take any lessons from anybody else?

Well, I took some lessons from Professor Dickinson. Yeah, I know you told me, but- A few lessons from him. Did you take lessons from any well-known? No, no. Maurice Duran was the one that coached me the most with the trophy.
This reminds me, did you ever go to the alley? Yeah, it was over here.
Yeah. Oh, a block from here. Yeah. That's where the market is.
Yeah.

Yeah, that was, uh, uh, oh, I see. Dominguez. A fellow by the name of Andre Dominguez used to run that place over there. The alley. You went over there? You went there? No, no, but I just heard about it. I'm-

That's right over there. I was a block from here. Yeah, block from here. Biggye Lillie and, and, and, uh, Bechet. Uh-huh. You know, I knew Professor Monetta, when he was teaching me. Yeah, yeah, yeah. He told me about all these different places. Yeah, uh-huh. And then I've been working-

Did you know him, too? Professor Melody, yeah. Manuel Monetta. Yes. Yeah, I know him. He, he played, uh, first time I met him, he was playing violin. Yeah. But he's a piano, he plays piano, and he plays trombone, and he plays cornet, too. Where did you hear him play? You heard him play in the district? No, I played in different places. Yeah. He played, uh, two trumpets together. Yeah, I've seen him. Uh, uh, how that's done, I don't know.
Uh-huh.
But he did it. And he played trombone, too. Uh-huh. He lived over in Andrew. Yes, I went to someone before he did.

Yeah. Yeah, I knew him good, too. I wanted to ask you something about, um, the musician's, um, position in society. Do you think that, uh, uh, people consider musicians as being, you know, far, uh, lower, high class people? Well, uh, some people think that they're low class people. And some people... I'm talking about a long time ago, aren't you?

Oh, well, they, they used to put you, you know, I might say, on the shelf. Yeah. If you was, uh, you know, worthwhile talking about, you know, I'd say, use the word like worthwhile. Uh-huh. Talking about it, they put you, they, they say, you know, you was good, you was alright, you was a good fellow.
You don't think that they looked down upon musicians? No, no, no, they never scorned them, you know, no. Before it being a, a bad job? No, they never scorned them.
You know, they had, uh...
Did your parents like that you were a musician?
Yeah, they, the only thing they didn't like, when I was practicing. Yeah.
They didn't like that at all. But, what, what, would they care like you what places you played in?
Oh, yeah, they, they liked it. I, you know, after I got, so that I could handle the instrument and do something with

it, they, they, they thought I was wonderful, you know. What about, before, when you said you went to the district, you know, the parents played out, didn't you? Well, but I didn't tell them, no, I didn't tell them. You must have told them that.
I didn't tell them that, no, see, I went, but I was telling them. Yeah.
What did your wife do?
Huh? Well, they, they, they couldn't watch me, because my old man was working that night. Yeah? Yeah, and they had too many other ones they wanted to, to mine, to watch, so they couldn't follow me.
Did your wife like to be able to sing it?
Yeah, she didn't mind. She tried to play piano, you know, like, too.
Oh, yeah? Oh, really? Did she go, ever go with you to your job, so could you ever take your wife with you to your job?

Yeah, I could go, that happened once or twice, but I never did go, because, uh, it, it, it, it made a, it made a sort of a confusion. Sometimes some women in the plays, you know, play for colored people, some women know you, you know, slightly, and they might come say something and tell you that, and your wife's out on the floor, and she's watching that, and she'd say, who's that woman that come up there? And, uh, so it's best not to bring up. What was your wife's name?
What was your wife's name? What's your wife's name?
Mabel, her name is Mabel. Uh-huh. She was a Mitchell, who I married. Uh-huh. Mabel Mitchell. Uh-huh.
You see, so it wasn't common to bring your wife on a job? No, no, I wouldn't.
I know I'd let her stay home.
You see, your Muslim citizens did that, huh? Huh? Muslim citizens did that. Yeah, yeah, it's better. Did you bring, like, their girlfriend sometime, or? Well, sometime you'd meet one day, yeah.
Yeah, I see. And they'd go ahead as far as you could, and when you had to knock off and go home, you had to tell them good night.
I mean, some places that you played, they wouldn't, maybe not allow you to bring other people with you.
Well, yeah, some places they have, they have their special invitation to you and another party. If you don't have no invitation, well, you could only come by yourself.
Like, did you ever play in the restaurants or places like that? No, I never did.
Peter used to play, you know? Yeah, I never had the chance to do none of that work.
What about boxing matches?
What about them, you mean?
Did you play at boxing matches? Oh, no.
You never played? No, I never played no boxing matches.
You ever played on the Boats?
I don't. Huh? Well, I played at the Capitol out there once. Yeah.
And they had a program for you, I understand. Ross was telling us about the program. On the Boats. Oh, you had to play so many numbers and all that and certain things?
Yeah, well, yeah, that's the way they had it. You played so much. It's planned. Yeah. Did you have programs like that in other places too?
No. I don't. Not that you played anyway.
No, no. You know the people in St. Louis knew what they were playing in New Orleans.
Yeah, they had a program they had to play.
Yeah. They had the Streckfuss family had that thing. The Streckfuss family, yeah.
They had the ones who had that thing in charge. Yeah, well, Vern is still alive. One of them was a violin player I made was a fan.
Yeah. I think they all fooled around with me.
Yeah. You played that job ever from, lasted from ten to six. How long were most jobs? How many hours were most jobs? Well, on them, on them, on these picnics practically all of them would like that.

Yeah, but I'm talking about other jobs. Oh, I had a job four hours, five hours. Yeah, they didn't usually last that long. Four, five hours, three hours sometimes. If you'd get a three hour one though you, you know, you'd feel something strange because it was a short time you had to work, three hours. Most of it was four hours, yeah.
But they started eight or nine or seven hours?
Well, you started, four hours, you started eight and worked until twelve, or you started nine and worked until one. Like that.
How did they used to give you intermission? How long intermission would they get?

Well, about ten, fifteen minutes you could walk around. Every hour? Every hour, yeah. That's pretty good. Yeah, that wasn't bad. That damn Jitney stuff was the worst thing I ever knew. That was the worst thing I ever knew. Yeah. But the other job was all right.
Some places that you played in, did they have like musicians rooms? Huh? Did they have a musicians room behind the stage?
Yeah, you had a place you could go sit down and rest up a little, you know.
But in all places you could always go out and mix in the crowd if you wanted to? Well, they never stopped you, you know.
If you can mix with the crowd.
I heard about some dance halls that they wouldn't let you go out and mix with them. Well, uh. For racial reasons. Yeah, that's right. Was there ever like that where you played?
Yeah. Yeah, I did. Some places like that. They wouldn't let you mix with them.
We'd mix with them. No.
I'm about to run out. You all let me run out? You run out of steam?
Yeah, I'm out of steam. I guess we got most of the information down there, we won't we?
Yeah, we're just about out of tape, so we appreciate it. Yeah, well, all right.
It was very nice talking to you.
Oh, I'm glad you all enjoyed it.
I enjoyed talking with you all. And you don't need this no more. No, no.
No, someday I'd like to copy the old one. Maybe copy the old one, yeah.
That one would be interesting to have for the old cast, I guess. Yeah, if we could get a camera. Maybe we could get a camera one day and take a picture of that. Yeah. Yeah, can you?
Yeah. You take it off of that?
Yeah, oh yeah, and then you have a safety. He has to put a strong light on it. Well, any time you get ready. Have a friend of mine have a good camera. Any time you get ready.
Yeah, Hans can do it and give him a copy. You can do it any time you get ready?
Yeah, because I'd like to keep it for the old cast. That's the only early picture we have of you. You're not in any band pictures.
No, you're not in any band pictures that we have.

You know, we have that manual parapses, they got big eyes on the band. Yeah, I know. They just put the instrument in the hand and all that stuff. Yeah. The whole instrument. I don't have no picture like that.
Do you remember them ever taking a picture of the band?
No, I don't remember.
I don't remember.
You had to go to a studio and all that in those days.
Yeah, well I told my wife one day this week, I was going to try to get this one taken.
Enlarge.
This one. This is the last one I got. Oh, we can get that enlarge for you.

Yeah. Hans might be able to do that. We might be able to do that. Yeah. We'll take the picture, maybe we can make it a bit. Yeah, well alright, that'd be good. What size do you want about that baby? Oh, alright, that'd be good. Something like that little baby there.

Right, yeah. That's my, my, that's my, that's my, that's my son. Oh, yeah. He's in the service. And that's, that's his daughter in the middle. And that's my great granddaughter. That's that good little daughter. You never made any recordings either then? No. No. 된 stuff with
Hmm. Well, the stuff is just... Yeah. Well, thank you again.

segments.title: Spelling the name LaCaze and starting the recording
segments.summary: Allen and LaCaze sort out the one-word spelling of the name and record the date.

segments.title: Mistaken for Peter Bocage; Amos Riley's parade band
segments.summary: LaCaze says people confused him with Peter Bocage, with whom he worked in street bands, and recalls playing second and third trumpet in Amos Riley's band.

segments.title: Birth in St. Bernard Parish and musicians from downriver
segments.summary: Born July 14, 1893 in St. Bernard Parish; parents spoke French among themselves; talk of musicians from the plantations downriver such as Jimmy Newman and the Durands.

segments.title: First violin and drums, then trumpet with Maurice Duran and Professor Nicholson
segments.summary: No one else in his family played; he tried violin in 1913, then trap drums, then learned trumpet fingering from Maurice Duran and studied with Professor Nicholson.

segments.title: Quitting the trumpet in 1934 because of gum disease
segments.summary: He played until 1934, when gum disease and poor pay made him give up music altogether.

segments.title: Parade bands, Joe Oliver and Louis Armstrong, and the shortage of players
segments.summary: He played with Oliver and Armstrong in parade bands; bands were always short of men, so almost anyone who could play got work and swapped between bands.

segments.title: Playing under Celestin with Armstrong, and lending his horn to Bunk Johnson
segments.summary: He played in the Tuxedo parade band with Louis Armstrong, loaned his instrument to Bunk Johnson for a Royal Garden dance, and listened to Storyville bands to learn from trumpeters.

segments.title: Favourite trumpeters: Armstrong and Manuel Perez, heard from the backyard
segments.summary: He liked Armstrong best, plus Manuel Perez, whose band he heard on Saturday nights from his backyard on Dauphine Street.

segments.title: Musicians of the Ninth Ward and downriver
segments.summary: Big Eye Louis and the Ninth Ward musicians (Duran, Joseph Watson, Charlie Bernard, Joe Hoodoo) and talk of players who went down to Delacroix Island.

segments.title: Henry Ford, violinist, and playing drums before trumpet
segments.summary: He knew two Henry Fords, played drums for about two years with the younger violinist, then switched to trumpet.

segments.title: Forming the Supreme Band with Eddie Jackson
segments.summary: His first trumpet band was the six-piece Supreme Band, organized with bass player Eddie Jackson, and it lasted a couple of years.

segments.title: Pianists and clarinetists in the Supreme Band
segments.summary: Trying to recall the band's woman pianist (Wilhelmina Barth is suggested) and clarinetist Arthur Williams.

segments.chapter: Nola band, day job and nightclub work
segments.title: After the Supreme Band: Ernest Johnson and dating the early bands
segments.summary: Bands drifted apart; he joined Ernest Johnson's band, and they try to date the Supreme Band.

segments.chapter: Nola band, day job and nightclub work
segments.title: Working hard on trumpet around a day job; the San Souci dance hall
segments.summary: He practiced evenings after day work, and the band played three nights a week at San Souci on Howard Street.

segments.chapter: Nola band, day job and nightclub work
segments.title: Nene Cuoco, 'Pills' and Henry Rush
segments.summary: He knew of Nene Cuoco, played a good while with crippled Pills, and counts drummer Henry Rush a friend.

segments.chapter: Nola band, day job and nightclub work
segments.title: The Nola Band, Ernest Johnson's band, Jack Carey and Punch Miller
segments.summary: Henry Rush was in the Nola Band; LaCaze stayed six to eight months with Ernest Johnson, then started the Nola Band, and played often with Jack Carey.

segments.chapter: Nola band, day job and nightclub work
segments.title: How long the Nola Band lasted and dating by the war
segments.summary: Hard to date; the Nola Band lasted until he quit in 1934; he never went to war.

segments.chapter: Nola band, day job and nightclub work
segments.title: Blacksmith day job (and one night on the Capitol boat)
segments.summary: From age seventeen he worked as a blacksmith with wagons and carriages until retirement; the trade was easier to find than music work and made playing hard. He also substituted once on the Capitol boat.

segments.chapter: Nola band, day job and nightclub work
segments.title: Nine-to-four nightclub job on Iberville and being fired for napping
segments.summary: Playing at Johnny Cialina's place from nine to four after day work lasted six months, until the band manager got him fired for napping.

segments.chapter: Nola band, day job and nightclub work
segments.title: Personnel and character of the Iberville nightclub band
segments.summary: The five-piece band had two saxophones, piano and drummer; LaCaze needed arrangements; the job was pitiful.

segments.chapter: Clubs, readers and musicians he knew
segments.title: The Music Box jitney dance at Carondelet and Canal
segments.summary: He worked a couple of weeks at the Music Box, a continuous jitney dance, replacing Arnold Metoyer.

segments.chapter: Clubs, readers and musicians he knew
segments.title: Asking about McCurdy, Lexis, Harrison Barnes and Red Allen
segments.summary: Allen asks whether he knew and played with Charles McCurdy, Ricard Alexis, Harrison Barnes and the Allens.

segments.chapter: Clubs, readers and musicians he knew
segments.title: Mercedes Gorman, Albert Baptiste and the Silver Leaf Band
segments.summary: Mercedes Gorman played in one of his bands; Albert Baptiste managed the Silver Leaf, which came before the Nola Band.

segments.chapter: Clubs, readers and musicians he knew
segments.title: Hippolyte Charles, the Dutreys, Pico and the Moreira family
segments.summary: He recalls Hippolyte Charles, Sam and Henry Dutrey, Alphonse Picou, Harrison Barnes in the Nola Band, and banjoist Lawrence Marrero and his brothers.

segments.chapter: Clubs, readers and musicians he knew
segments.title: Reading music and carrying orchestrations to jobs
segments.summary: He was not a sight-reader but learned parts between tunes, and always brought orchestrations to jobs.

segments.chapter: Clubs, readers and musicians he knew
segments.title: Scott Joplin, favorite numbers and which musicians could read
segments.summary: Talk of Joplin orchestrations, Sonny Henry's reading, and bands like Piron's and Robichaux's that had readers.

segments.chapter: Clubs, readers and musicians he knew
segments.title: The many 'T-Boys'
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about saxophonist and trumpeters nicknamed T-Boy, including Dominique Remy and Paul Barbarin.

segments.chapter: Youth, Storyville and the bands he heard
segments.title: Why he took up music at 14, his father's work and dislike of jitney dances
segments.summary: He wanted to play after hearing music at 14 and worked in a blacksmith shop; his father delivered wholesale meat; he played for love, not money.

segments.chapter: Youth, Storyville and the bands he heard
segments.title: Early drumming and Freddie Gould
segments.summary: Drummed with Henry Ford; knew guitarist Freddie Gould from the Ninth Ward but never played with him.

segments.chapter: Youth, Storyville and the bands he heard
segments.title: First bands he heard: Perez and William Moreira
segments.summary: The first band he heard had Manuel Perez on trumpet and a valve trombone; also William Moreira's band.

segments.chapter: Youth, Storyville and the bands he heard
segments.title: Personnel and instrumentation of the Superior band
segments.summary: Players in Billy Moreira's Superior band, and use of guitars, banjos, pianos, violins and string bass in early small bands.

segments.chapter: Youth, Storyville and the bands he heard
segments.title: Carnival clubs, addresses he lived at, and his 1914 marriage
segments.summary: He never played carnival parades; lists where he lived; married in 1914 when just starting trumpet.

segments.chapter: Youth, Storyville and the bands he heard
segments.title: Hearing a trumpeter in Storyville who encouraged him
segments.summary: A nice trumpet player in a small Storyville group encouraged him; bands were on every corner.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: The Humphrey family and other trombonists
segments.summary: He played with Willie and Earl Humphrey, comments on Earl's trombone, and on Zue Robertson and Frankie Duson.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Sam Morgan's two bands and the Imperial band
segments.summary: Sam Morgan's first band with Alfred on drums was best; Joe Watson may have been in it; they used some music.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Perez's band: repertoire of reading bands, waltzes, quadrilles and polkas
segments.summary: A reading band played ragtime, waltzes, schottisches, quadrilles and polkas, whereas Sam Morgan played mostly popular songs.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Blues, and hymns by brass bands
segments.summary: Bands played blues without music, learned first because of few notes; only brass bands played hymns.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Kid Thomas and George Lewis
segments.summary: Kid Thomas was well regarded with a good variety band; George Lewis was a good clarinetist who worked with everybody.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Chris Kelly and filling his jobs
segments.summary: He played jobs for Chris Kelly when Kelly was double-booked; Kelly did not read.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Violins in New Orleans bands
segments.summary: Violin was used only when a clarinet or sax was unavailable; bands relied on trumpet and clarinet.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Buddy Petit and the violinist Joseph Welch
segments.summary: He knew Buddy Petit and liked his playing, and recalls violinist Joseph Welch.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Manuel Ridgley and the Pelican dance hall
segments.summary: He played upstairs at the Pelican, run by Manuel Ridgley, with the Silver Leaf and Nola bands; Royal Garden and Astoria nearby.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Looking for old photographs
segments.summary: No band pictures survive; a recent picture from May 1970 is looked at. Passage partly repeats due to transcription.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Hippolyte Charles, Sweet Emma and who ran the Silver Leaf
segments.summary: He recalls Albert Baptiste ran the Silver Leaf, Hippolyte Charles and Sweet Emma may have been in it, and Henry Russ played with it.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: Sam Dutrey Sr., Arthur Williams and Camilla Todd
segments.summary: Sam Dutrey Sr. played with LaCaze often; Arthur Williams was a clarinetist; Camilla Todd a pianist he worked with.

segments.chapter: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
segments.title: The Capitol boat: a strict reading band
segments.summary: His one night on the Capitol was a reading band using stock arrangements; only three or four bands he knew had special arrangements.

segments.title: Battles of bands at the Pelican and out-of-town bands
segments.summary: At the Pelican two bands sometimes played opposite each other; Bebe Ridley, Clarence Williams and Bud Scott are asked about.

segments.title: Autocrat Club, Bulls Club and other clubs
segments.summary: He played regularly at the Autocrat, Bulls Club and San Souci, mostly for dancing.

segments.title: Summer jobs at Spanish Fort, West End and Milneburg camps
segments.summary: Outdoor pavilion jobs at lakefront camps ran ten to six on Sundays, with food and about six dollars.

segments.title: Lucien's Pavilion and Milneburg
segments.summary: He played once at Lucien's Pavilion near Milneburg, used for banquets.

segments.title: Ninth Ward trades, musicians' day jobs and trappers
segments.summary: Many musicians lived on music alone; Ninth Ward trades and the Moss Pickers and Coon Trappers club.

segments.title: Fights, shootings and an injured trumpeter
segments.summary: Fights were rare; once in St. John Parish shooting broke out; Ricard Alexis was beaten and lost his embouchure.

segments.title: The musicians' union
segments.summary: He never belonged to a union, which was weak and ineffective then.

segments.title: Playing outside the city
segments.summary: He played Jefferson and St. Charles Parishes and Mississippi but rarely left the state, partly due to his day job.

segments.title: Advertising wagons and the old market
segments.summary: He played drums on advertising wagons; description of the open market.

segments.title: The WPA band and not getting in
segments.summary: He quit about when the WPA band started; trying to get in was a matter of politics.

segments.title: Who got hired: readers, politics, and audiences hating music racks
segments.summary: Hiring turned on need and ability to read, though crowds disliked bands seen with sheet music.

segments.title: Playing for white and Black audiences: pay and treatment
segments.summary: He mostly played white places with better pay and treatment; Black venues lacked money.

segments.title: The Irish Channel dances
segments.summary: With Ernest Johnson he played Irish Channel dances; trouble was stopped by music.

segments.title: Germans, Creoles and Creole singers
segments.summary: He played for Irish, calls himself Creole but cannot speak it, and discusses Creole singers.

segments.title: Singing choruses and lung damage from soldering fumes
segments.summary: He sang choruses through paper megaphones until fumes damaged his lungs.

segments.title: Creole musicians and mixed Creole bands
segments.summary: Duran and Perez were Creoles; he played with any kind of musicians.

segments.title: Louis Cottrell, the Magnolia Band, Freddie Keppard and popularity
segments.summary: He played occasionally with Louis Cottrell and admired Freddie Keppard, popular in the Olympia band.

segments.title: Most popular trumpeters: Armstrong, Oliver and Rena
segments.summary: Armstrong most popular, then Joe Oliver and Kid Rena, popular regardless of section. Transcript ends with ASR loop.

segments.title: Black and white audiences and feeling out the crowd
segments.summary: No musicians played only for Black audiences; bands tested tunes on the crowd, and people wanted common music.

segments.title: Clubs, societies and selling insurance
segments.summary: He joined no clubs, and sold insurance for Unity at one time.

segments.title: Light-skinned musicians passing in white bands
segments.summary: Light-skinned Black musicians such as Arnold Metoyer and Eddie Cherrie played in white bands; Achille Baquet.

segments.title: Listening around and lessons from Dickinson and Maurice Duran
segments.summary: He learned by going around listening; Duran coached him most.

segments.title: The Alley, Dominguez and Professor Manetta
segments.summary: Andre Dominguez ran the Alley; Manuel Manetta played violin, piano, trombone and cornet.

segments.title: Social standing of musicians and his parents' reaction
segments.summary: Musicians were not scorned; his parents disliked practicing but approved later.

segments.title: His wife Mabel and not bringing her to jobs
segments.summary: His wife Mabel Mitchell stayed home; places played at were not restaurants.

segments.title: Boxing matches and the Streckfus steamer program
segments.summary: He never played boxing matches; the boat had planned programs.

segments.title: Length of jobs, intermissions and mixing with the crowd
segments.summary: Jobs lasted four hours with fifteen-minute breaks; jitney the worst.

segments.title: Closing remarks and a photograph
segments.summary: Tape ends; they discuss copying his photograph; no recordings made.
